label: lem:integral_is_antiderivative
title: The integral function is an antiderivative
statement: Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[\min(a,b), \max(a,b)]$. Define the integral function $G : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $G(u) = \int_a^u f(t)\,dt$. Then $G$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on the open interval $(\min(a,b), \max(a,b))$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:antiderivative}. That is, $\texttt{HasDerivAt}\; G\; (f\; x)\; x$ holds for every $x \in (\min(a,b), \max(a,b))$.
proof: This is an immediate consequence of the First Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Theorem~\ref{thm:ftc1}), which establishes that $G$ has derivative $f(x)$ at every interior point $x$. By Definition~\ref{def:antiderivative}, this precisely means that $G$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on the open interval.
